summary: Sirach 34 warns against trusting dreams, divinations, and fantasies unless they are truly sent by the Most High. It contrasts empty hopes with wisdom gained through instruction, experience, travel, and fear of the Lord. The chapter then turns sharply against sacrifices funded by injustice, especially by taking from the poor or withholding a worker's pay.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins two concerns central to Sirach: wise discernment and ethical worship. It insists that reverence for God cannot be separated from truthfulness, care for the poor, and changed conduct.

context.author: Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted instruction shaped by Israel's law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with the temple and priesthood central to worship and Jewish scribes teaching wisdom within a Greek-speaking Mediterranean world.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in compact poetic sayings and comparisons.

outline.heading: Dreams and false hopes
outline.note: The teacher warns that dreams, divinations, and soothsayings can mislead unless they come from the Most High, while truthful wisdom fulfills the law.

outline.heading: Experience and instruction
outline.note: Knowledge is linked with instruction, experience, travel, danger, and what the speaker has learned through life.

outline.heading: Hope in the Lord
outline.note: Those who fear the Lord are described as living with hope, support, protection, and blessing from him.

outline.heading: Unjust offerings rejected
outline.note: Sacrifices taken from wrongdoing or from the poor are called mockery and compared to bloodshed.

outline.heading: Prayer without change
outline.note: The chapter closes with actions that undo or oppose one another: one person builds while another tears down, one prays while another curses, and cleansing or fasting is undone by renewed defilement or repeated sin.

keyVerses.text: If they are not sent in a visitation from the Most High, don’t give your heart to them.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter's limit on dreams: they are not treated as reliable simply because they feel significant.

keyVerses.text: The spirit of those who fear the Lord will live, for their hope is in him who saves them.
keyVerses.why: It marks the turn from unreliable hopes to hope placed in the Lord.

keyVerses.text: The bread of the needy is the life of the poor. He who deprives him of it is a man of blood.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's strongest statement that taking from the poor is not a minor fault but an attack on life.

keyVerses.text: Even so a man fasting for his sins, and going again, and doing the same, who will listen to his prayer? What profit does he have in his humiliation?
keyVerses.why: The final verse sums up the warning against religious practice that is not joined to changed conduct.

themes: fear of the Lord as hope

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by warning about dreams?
questions.answer: The chapter says dreams can give false confidence to a person without understanding. It does not deny every possible divine visitation, but it warns readers not to give their heart to dreams unless they are sent by the Most High.

questions.question: Does Sirach say all dreams are useless?
questions.answer: No. Verse 6 leaves room for a dream sent in a visitation from the Most High. The warning is against treating dreams, divinations, and soothsayings as trustworthy sources when they are vain or false.

questions.question: What does “vain” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “vain” describes hopes, divinations, soothsayings, and dreams that cannot reliably guide a person. The word is tied to what is empty, misleading, or unable to produce truth.

questions.question: Why does the teacher value travel and experience?
questions.answer: The chapter says a well-instructed person knows many things, and a person with much experience can declare understanding. Travel is presented as one way experience increases cleverness, though the speaker also says it involved danger.

questions.question: What does “fear the Lord” look like here?
questions.answer: The chapter describes those who fear the Lord as people whose hope is in him. It says they will not be afraid or cowardly, and it pictures the Lord as their protection, support, guard, and help.

questions.question: Why are some sacrifices called mockery?
questions.answer: The problem is not sacrifice itself but sacrifice connected to wrongdoing. The chapter says an offering from something wrongfully gotten is mockery and that the Most High has no pleasure in offerings from the ungodly.

questions.question: Why does the chapter speak so strongly about taking from the poor?
questions.answer: It says the bread of the needy is the life of the poor, so depriving them is treated as violence against life. The same logic is applied to taking away a neighbor's living or withholding a hireling's hire.

questions.question: What is the point of the examples about washing, fasting, and doing the same thing again?
questions.answer: The closing comparisons show actions that oppose one another or are undone by repetition. Washing after touching a dead body means little if the person touches it again, and fasting for sins is questioned if the person goes back to doing the same thing.

glossary.def: In this chapter, dreams are treated as unreliable guides when they become a basis for false hope, unless they are sent by the Most High.
A title for God used here when speaking about a possible divine visitation and about God's rejection of unjust offerings.
A paid worker; the chapter says depriving a hireling of his hire is like shedding blood.
The self-lowering associated here with fasting for sins; the chapter questions its value when a person returns to the same conduct.
